en: Preface to the Re-engraving of the *Cundī-jingye* I have often heard it said:
"There is a substance prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It can act as the sovereign of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither along with the four seasons.

This indeed is the source of the myriad forms that lack physical shape—the secret and profound mystery of the nature-school (*xingzong*)—and that which the sages of the Three Teachings [have realized].
Regarding those who cannot transcend [this]: Later Zhao’s Lord Wen-su drew a single circle (○) and called it the "Diagram of the Primordial Chaos" (*hun-yuan-tú*).
He further added a *svastika* within it (☶) and called it the "Diagram of the Wheel-Phase of the Myriad Characters.

I have reflected upon this three times and privately maintain that it represents both true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*). It is the state where the one is the immeasurable, and the immeasurable is the one. Why?

I alone harbored doubts regarding the pure practice of Cundī. On the winter solstice of the year Wumu (1658), I dreamed that Master Luo Jinxi showed me a circular diagram and said, "Your eyes are clear and sharp; if you constantly contemplate this, you will enter the Way with great speed.
He then spoke to a monk, who handed me two divination slips. I looked at the slips and saw the character "Nan" (South) on them. Startled, I thought, "This is my teacher."
He wept until his tears soaked his breast-cloth. Upon waking, he was struck with a sense of alarm, not knowing what it all meant.

Shortly thereafter, a monk named De’an arrived, holding a petition to solicit donations for the casting of a statue of the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara. I explained that the word "qian" (thousand) and "qian" (lot) were phonetically similar.
Is this not what is meant by the "Thousand Hands and Thousand Eyes" of Great Compassion? Upon further inquiry, it was found that he was proficient in Sanskrit mantras.
Furthermore, he was able to write the *Cundī* mantra in Sanskrit characters, which he stated was transmitted by eminent monks from the Western Regions;

it was a genuine version that perfectly accorded with the Sanskrit and Tibetan originals, and thus worthy of trust. Consequently, he drew a circular moon disc and inscribed the nine sacred Sanskrit syllables within it.
All were exquisite and delightful. I recall that on a night long past, I dreamed that Master Jinxi showed me a circular diagram;
though it contained no written characters, how could the characters ever have been absent from within it? Now, this monk has bestowed the Sanskrit script upon me.
Although these words have been set down in writing, they are devoid of any characteristics of written characters. This is indeed the teaching long established by our late master, Tangnan.
Previously, Master Tang visited Master Jin’eng, and they discussed the merits of Cundi. Upon returning, he spoke of this to the Imperial Censor He Shaolong.

From then on, he took these instructions to heart and never forgot them; however, he remained solely in doubt regarding the Sanskrit characters.

The nine sacred Sanskrit characters are, in their very essence, the Dharma-realm of Vairocana; the six and eight gates of aspiration are, in their very essence, the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices.

If external conditions are not fulfilled—such as having no water for bathing or lacking fresh, clean clothing—one should purify oneself using only this syllable *laṃ*. If external conditions are fulfilled, one first uses water and puts on fresh, clean clothing, and then further purifies oneself with this syllable *laṃ*. Thus...
[This means that both the internal and external are completely purified]. Next, recite the *rakṣā-mantra* twenty-one times.
The *rakṣā-mantra* is *oṃ kili kili*. (The character *kili* is pronounced with a departing tone; this is the Sanskrit script for *oṃ kili*).
This mantra can extinguish all karmic offenses of the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
It can eliminate all manner of suffering from illness, calamities, obstacles, evil dreams, malevolent spirits, ghosts, demons, and all inauspicious events.
It can accomplish all superior matters and cause every aspiration to be fully realized. This mantra is the heart-essence of all Buddhas. If a person...
Reciting it once with single-minded devotion can protect one’s own person; all ghosts, spirits, celestial Māras, and demons will dare not approach.
Reciting it twice can protect one’s companions. Reciting it three times can protect everyone within a single household.
Reciting it four times can protect everyone within a single city, and so on, up to seven times, which can protect the four continents of the world.
[The practitioner] (the first two mantras may each be recited one hundred and eight times as well). Next, recite the Six-Syllable Great Illumination Mantra one hundred and eight times.
The Six-Syllable Great Illumination Mantra is:
Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ. (These are the six syllables in Sanskrit script.)
If one recites this mantra, wherever one dwells, there will assemble immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
Furthermore, it possesses immeasurable gates of samādhi and dharmas. For the person who recites and upholds it, seven generations of their lineage shall all attain liberation;
the various worms within their abdomen shall attain the rank of Bodhisattva, and this person shall daily become fully endowed with [virtues].
Through the perfection of the six pāramitās and the fulfillment of merit, one attains an immeasurable accumulation of pure wisdom and eloquence.
When the breath exhaled from one’s mouth touches the bodies of others, those who are touched are freed from all poisonous anger and shall attain the rank of a bodhisattva.
Even if all the people of the four continents were to attain the rank of a bodhisattva of the seventh stage, those [who are touched]— [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]
All the merits possessed by a bodhisattva are equal to, and no different from, the merit of reciting this six-syllable mantra once.
This mantra is the subtle and wondrous fundamental mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
If a person transcribes this six-syllable vidyā-mantra, the merit obtained is equal to that of transcribing the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma; they are no different.

It is different. If one were to fashion images of the Tathāgata out of gold and jewels as numerous as motes of dust, it would not equal the merit of even a single syllable among these six characters written down.
If a person obtains this six-syllable Great Mantra (ṣaḍakṣarī vidyā), they cannot be defiled by greed, anger, or delusion.
Furthermore, those who wear and maintain this mantra upon their bodies will likewise not be defiled by greed, anger, or delusion.

Illness. Any sentient being touched by the hands or body, or seen by the eyes, of this wearer and holder shall swiftly attain the rank of a Bodhisattva and never again undergo the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

When these six syllables of the Great Illuminator (Mahāvidyā) were finished being spoken, seventy-seven koṭis of Buddhas appeared simultaneously before him and, with one voice, recited the Cundī Dhāraṇī.
One should then know that these six-syllable vidyā-mantra and the Cundī-dhāraṇī are required in successive order.
Thereafter, one should form the Cundī-mudrā at the heart; then, with the Cundī-dhāraṇī and the Ekākṣara-cakravartin-mantra, [one should proceed].

Recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times together. Scatter the hand-seal (mudrā) upon the crown of the head. (Alternatively, for those who do not prefer the Mahāvidyārājñī Dhāraṇī, it is also sufficient to hold only the Cundī Mantra.

Regarding the method for the Cundī seal: interlace the ring fingers and little fingers of both hands within. Straighten the middle fingers of both hands so they support each other. Bend the two index fingers and attach them to the first joints of the middle fingers.

With the two thumbs, pinch the middle joints of the right hand’s ring fingers. If there is an invocation, move the two index fingers back and forth. While correctly forming the seal and reciting the mantra, when wishing to keep count, mark it upon the fingers of one's own body—or, [mark it] on the Cundī [image].)

It may be marked on the forearm of the Bodhisattva, or it may be marked upon the heart of the Avalokiteśvara; either way, it is acceptable. It is even better if one forms the mudrā and recites the mantra one thousand and eighty times, or at least one hundred and eight times.

Alternatively, one may simply hold the rosary with the left hand while forming the Vajra-fist mudrā with the right hand and counting the beads. For those who are busy, it is sufficient to hold it loosely.
The Great Cundī Dhāraṇī of the Heart of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas (also known as the One-Syllable Mahācakra Mantra; to be recited together with the following):
Namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭinām | Tadyathā | Oṃ cale cule cunde svāhā | Pūleṃ ||
(These are the two *dhāraṇīs* of Cundī in Sanskrit script.
The Buddha said: "This *dhāraṇī* can extinguish all karmic obstacles of the ten non-virtues and the five heinous crimes, and bring to fulfillment all pure dharmas and meritorious virtues.
For those who uphold this *dhāraṇī*, whether they be laypeople or monastics, even if they drink alcohol, eat meat, or have a wife,"
Child, without discriminating between purity and impurity, simply recite with a sincere heart; this can cause short-lived sentient beings to increase their lifespan immeasurably.
Even the disease of kāmalā (jaundice) can be cured, let alone other ailments. It is impossible that it would not be extinguished.
If you recite for a full forty-nine days, Bodhisattva Cundī will cause the two sages to constantly follow you.
Whatever thoughts of good or evil that person has will all be reported to them, one by one, right by their ear.
If there are those who lack merit or auspicious signs, who fail to attain office despite seeking it, or who are oppressed by poverty and suffering, they should constantly recite this mantra;

it can cause them to obtain the blessings of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) in the present life, and whatever official rank they seek will surely be attained as desired. (Cited from the *Chanzong chuanteng lu*).

People say: "Juiti (Kubjita) merely recited three lines of mantra, yet he became renowned as one who transcends all others. If one seeks wisdom, one obtains great wisdom; if one seeks sons or daughters, one obtains sons or daughters.
Whatever one seeks, there is nothing that is not fulfilled accordingly. It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), granting everything according to one's heart's desire.
Furthermore, by reciting this mantra, one can cause kings, ministers, and the four classes of living beings to develop affection [for oneself].
With a heart of reverence, upon seeing this person who recites this mantra, one shall immediately rejoice. Such a person cannot be drowned by water, nor burned by fire.
Neither poisons, enemies, military arrays, powerful bandits, nor evil dragons, beasts, and various malevolent spirits can cause them any harm.
If you wish to invite Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, Yama-rāja, or others, simply recite this mantra;
they will surely arrive as invited. They will not dare to disregard your summons, and all tasks you entrust to them shall be accomplished according to your will.
This mantra possesses great power within Jambudvīpa; it can move Mount Sumeru, dry up the waters of the great ocean, and parch it to desiccation.

A tree can produce flowers and fruit; how much more so, then, for one who further recites the mantra according to the ritual? Without changing their physical body, they shall attain great supernormal powers and go to the Tuṣita Heaven.
If one seeks longevity or various elixirs of the immortals, it is sufficient simply to recite the mantra according to the ritual.
One will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva or Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, who will bestow a wondrous elixir of the immortals.
Upon taking it as prescribed, one will immediately attain the path of the immortals, prolonging one's lifespan to equal that of the sun and moon, and realize the rank of a bodhisattva.
If one recites this according to the ritual until it reaches one million times, one will then be able to travel to the pure lands of the ten directions.
Having served various Buddhas and universally heard the wondrous Dharma, one attains the realization of Bodhi.
The One-Syllable Mantra of the Great Wheel is precisely this *Kūṣmāṇḍa* (transliterated as *bu-lin*). It is also called the One-Syllable Heart-Mantra of the Final Dharma Age (*mofa*).
During the time of the Final Dharma, when the Dharma is about to perish, this mantra possesses great power and can [act] within the world.
It brings about great benefit. It can protect the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata;
it can subdue all the eight classes of supernatural beings; it can destroy all evil spells of the world.
It is the crown of all Buddhas and the heart of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. It can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings and grant them...
It is blissful. For all who practice it, they shall obtain results according to their wishes, just like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), capable of fulfilling every aspiration.
If one recites this mantra, within a radius of five hundred *yojanas* in the four directions, all malevolent spirits and ghosts will disperse on their own;
no evil planetary deities or celestial Māras shall dare to approach. If one maintains and recites it for even one [day]...
If one fears that any mantra will not achieve accomplishment, one should immediately employ this spell together with other mantras, reciting and upholding them in one place.
If it is certain that accomplishment is not attained and no manifest efficacy appears, the deities of that spell shall have their heads split into seven pieces.
Thus it is known that this spell can assist all mantras, enabling swift attainment of accomplishment.

(Alternatively, it is also permissible to recite this mantra separately. Having recited the preceding mantras in sequence up to the Cundī-mantra, if one is unable to perform the Cundī mudrā, one should simply form the Vajra-fist mudrā with the left hand while holding the rosary with the right hand and reciting it.
Alternatively, for those who are unable to recite the preceding *dhāraṇīs* of the Pure Dharma Realm and so forth in their proper sequence, they may simply hold the Cundī Dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, for those of dull faculties who cannot fully receive this Cundī, they may simply hold the portion from the syllable "Oṃ" onwards.
The portion prior to the syllable "Oṃ" consists of words of refuge and homage; the syllable "Oṃ" and what follows are the actual mantra. At each [recitation],...
Having completed the recitation, then form the Vajra Fist mudrā with the right hand and recite the mantra of the syllable HŪṂ while sealing the five places:
first seal the forehead, next the left and right shoulders, next the heart, and finally seal the throat;
then release the mudrā upon the crown of the head. This can eliminate all demonic obstacles and accomplish all supreme matters.
Dedicate the merit and make vows as previously described, reciting them according to one’s inclination.

Continue with the Pure Practice liturgy (according to the *Cundī-sūtra*, after completing the recitation of the mantra and the dedication of merit, one may walk about at will or read Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; therefore, continue the liturgical practice here).
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom:
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and distress.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness.
Emptiness is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Śāriputra, this mark of emptiness of all phenomena is neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, in emptiness there is no form;
no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; and no sphere of the eye.
...up to and including the sphere of consciousness. There is no ignorance, nor is there the end of ignorance.

Up to and including old age and death, there is no old age and death, nor is there the end of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom, nor is there attainment.
Because there is nothing to be attained, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no mental hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no...
There is fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the unequaled mantra.
It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. Therefore, I shall now proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī.
The dhāraṇī is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation," the Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra:
1. Paying homage to all Buddhas; 2. Praising the Tathāgatas; 3. Extensively cultivating offerings;
4. Repenting of karmic obstructions; 5. Rejoicing in merit; 6. Requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma; 7. Requesting the Buddhas [to remain].
To abide in the world; eighth, to constantly follow and learn from the Buddha; ninth, to always accord with sentient beings; tenth, to universally dedicate [all merit].
May all roots of goodness—those of prostration, praise, and making offerings; those of requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma;
those of sympathetic joy and repentance—be dedicated to sentient beings and to the path of Buddhahood.
May I, at the time when my life draws to a close, Be completely freed from all obstacles,
And behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, Thereby attaining rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once I have been reborn in that land, May this great vow be fulfilled before me.
All perfections were complete without exception; he brought benefit and happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings.
That Buddha’s assembly was entirely pure, and at that time, I personally beheld the Tathāgata Amitābha born from a supreme lotus, who conferred upon me the prophecy of awakening in his very presence.
Having received this prophecy from that Tathāgata, his emanations number in the hundreds of koṭis;

with vast power of wisdom pervading the ten directions, he universally benefits the realms of all sentient beings until the end of empty space and the exhaustion of sentient beings, karma, and afflictions.
As long as all these remain inexhaustible, may my vow likewise endure forever without end.
This sublime conduct of Samantabhadra and its boundless, supreme merit, I dedicate entirely:
may all sentient beings who are submerged in suffering swiftly proceed to the buddha-field of Amitābha.

In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, in the chapter on "Birth in the Highest Grade of the Highest Class," the Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Regarding birth in the highest grade of the highest class:
if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, they shall attain rebirth by giving rise to three kinds of minds. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second..."
The mind of profound resolve; third, the mind of dedication and aspiration. Those who possess these three minds will certainly be born in that land.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth there. What are these three? First, those who possess a heart of loving-kindness and do not kill, being fully endowed with all precepts and practices.
Second, those who read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. Third, those who practice the six remembrances and dedicate [their merit] toward [rebirth].
He makes a vow, wishing to be born in that land. Endowed with these merits, after one day up to seven days, he shall immediately attain rebirth there.

At the time of his birth in that land, because this person has been diligent and courageous, Amitābha Tathāgata, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, the great assembly of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and the seven... [heavenly beings].
The precious palace hall. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, holding a vajra platform, together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, arrives before the practitioner.
Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body; together with the various bodhisattvas, he extends his hand to welcome them.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, along with countless bodhisattvas, praise the practitioner and urge them forward.

The practitioner, having seen this, rejoices and leaps for joy. Seeing himself mounted upon a vajra pedestal, following behind the Buddha, he is reborn in that land in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
Having been born in that land, he beholds the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all its marks;
he beholds the bodhisattvas, complete with their physical characteristics; and he sees the jewel groves radiating light as they proclaim the sublime Dharma. Upon hearing this, he immediately—

They realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In the space of a mere moment, they attend upon various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, receiving successive predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) in the presence of those Buddhas.
Returning to their own land, they attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates.
This is called the highest birth of the superior grade.
The Divine Mantra for Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstructions and Rebirth in the Pure Land:
*Namo amitābhāya tathāgatāya | tadyathā | amṛtodbhave amṛtāṣṭhāne amṛtavikaraṇe amṛte...*
RIDDHI-VIKARAṆA-GAMINI GAGANA-CITTA-KĀRI SVĀHĀ (The syllable *dhi* is pronounced with a departing tone, like *duo* or *dai*;
either way is acceptable). The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color;
His marks and signs, and his radiant light, are peerless.
The white curl of hair winds like five Mount Sumerus; The deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And the hosts of transformed Bodhisattvas are likewise boundless.
With forty-eight vows to deliver sentient beings, He causes those of all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
Namo Amitābha Buddha (recite one thousand times, or three hundred to five hundred times, or ten recitations).
Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (ten recitations).
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta (ten times).
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly (ten times).
Dedication Prayer for the Western Direction.
I prostrate to the Great Teacher of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, who receives and guides all sentient beings.
Now I make this vow to be reborn there; may you, out of compassion, graciously accept me, [Name], your disciple.
For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all beings in the Dharma-realm, I seek the One Vehicle of all Buddhas.

Because the path to unsurpassed bodhi is so difficult to traverse, one should single-mindedly hold in mind and recite the sublime name of Amitābha Buddha, which possesses ten thousand virtues, with the aspiration to be born in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, because karmic burdens are heavy and blessings are meager, hindrances are deep and wisdom is shallow; defiled thoughts easily flare up while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish.
Now, before reciting the Buddha’s name, with body prostrate in diligent devotion and heart laid bare in total sincerity, I repent.
And for all sentient beings: from vast eons until the present, we have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind. We have indulged in greed, anger, and ignorance, defiling the three karmas;
may all the immeasurable and boundless stains of sin committed, and the immeasurable and boundless karmic debts of enmity incurred, be entirely extinguished.
From this day forward, we establish profound vows to distance ourselves from unwholesome dharmas and vow never to create them again, diligently practicing [the path].
The Noble Path. I vow not to retreat or become indolent. I vow to attain perfect enlightenment. I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
May Amitābha Buddha, by the power of his compassionate vows, bear witness to me; may he take pity on me; may he bestow his grace upon me.
I pray that within my meditative contemplation and during my dreams, I may behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha and traverse through...
In the land adorned with jewels of Amitābha Buddha, may I receive the empowerment of the nectar of Amitābha Buddha’s light, which shines upon my body;

may his hand stroke my head and his robe cover my form, causing my karmic obstructions to be spontaneously removed, my roots of goodness to increase, my afflictions to be swiftly emptied, and ignorance to be suddenly shattered.
May the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment be fully awakened, and the realm of tranquil light—
The true realm will constantly manifest before them. When the time approaches for their life to end, they will know in advance that it has arrived;
their bodies will be free from all illness, suffering, and calamities, and their minds will be free from all attachment and delusion.

Their faculties will be joyful and serene, their right mindfulness clear and distinct, and they will cast off their retribution with composure, as if entering meditative absorption. Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, will appear before them.
The assembly of all noble sages emitted light to welcome and guide us; they reached down with their hands to lead us.
With multi-storied pavilions, banners, and pennants, and with extraordinary fragrances and celestial music, the sacred realm of the West was revealed before our very eyes.
All sentient beings who saw or heard this were filled with joy and wonder, and they resolved to attain Bodhicitta. At that time, I mounted a vajra pedestal and followed behind the Buddha. As...
In the space of a finger-snap, one is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within a pond of the seven treasures, amidst a magnificent lotus flower, the flower opens to reveal the Buddha;

one beholds the various Bodhisattvas and hears the wondrous sound of the Dharma, thereby attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). In an instant, one serves all Buddhas and personally receives their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Having received this prediction, one attains the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), [endowed with] the immeasurable...
Having fully accomplished hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates and all meritorious virtues, they shall not remain apart from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*),
but shall return to the Sahā world. There, manifesting countless bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions,
they will deliver sentient beings through inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers and various skillful means, causing them all to leave defilement behind and regain a pure mind.
May we be born together in the Western Land and enter the stage of non-retrogression.

With such great vows as these, may the worlds be inexhaustible, sentient beings be inexhaustible, karma and afflictions be entirely inexhaustible, and my own vow be inexhaustible. Now, I prostrate to the Buddha and make this aspiration.
May the merit cultivated through these practices be dedicated to all sentient beings. May the four debts of gratitude be fully repaid and the three realms of existence be equally sustained.
May all beings throughout the Dharma-realm together realize the wisdom of the All-Knowing One.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings lead great assemblies with total unimpededness. Homage to the Holy Ones.

If one has further capacity, one should also fully recite them.]
Regarding the Dharma Gate of the Ten Recitations:
in this world, there are those who are extremely busy and have not a moment’s leisure; for such people, they must perform the ten recitations every morning at dawn.
As for the ten recitations: at early dawn, facing west, stand upright with palms joined and chant "Amitābha Buddha" continuously until the count of ten is complete.
One breath constitutes one recitation. Ten such breaths are called ten recitations. One should simply follow the length of the breaths without limiting the number of Buddhas;
the aim is only to make them long and enduring, with the breath reaching its full extent as the measure.

The sound of the Buddha’s name should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too fast, but balanced and moderate. These ten breaths should be continuous and uninterrupted, the mind focused upon—
To cause the mind not to be distracted and to apply oneself with single-minded diligence is why this is called "ten recitations. This demonstrates that it relies on the breath to bind the mind.
Throughout this entire life, one must not abandon these ten recitations for even a single day. Upon completion, one should perform the dedication of merit and make a vow, saying:
I, [Name], disciple, with single-minded devotion take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May your pure light illuminate me;
may your compassionate vow embrace me. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata for the sake of the path to Bodhi, seeking birth in the Pure Land.
According to the Buddha’s original vow: "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land, and who with sincere heart believe and rejoice..."
If, even with ten recitations of my name, one does not attain birth [in the Pure Land], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

By virtue of these causes and conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one enters the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows; sustained by the power of the Buddha’s compassion, all transgressions are extinguished.

The causes for purification increase. When approaching the end of life, one knows for oneself that the time has come; the body is free from the suffering of illness, the mind is without craving or attachment, and there is no delusion.
As if entering meditative absorption, the Buddhas and the assembly of sages arrive to welcome one, holding golden platforms in their hands.

In a single thought-moment, one is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon the opening of the lotus flower, one beholds the Buddha and immediately hears the Buddha-vehicle, attaining sudden [enlightenment].
Opening the Buddha’s wisdom. Universally delivering sentient beings. Fulfilling the vows of Bodhi.

The Ritual Manual for Contemplative Practice (Based on the Essentials of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings; following the Great Mantra of Cundī, this specifically highlights contemplative practice as taught in various sutras—namely, the method of dual cultivation of exoteric and esoteric practices).

[Note: The previous version focused exclusively on recitation while omitting contemplative practice for the sake of easy dissemination; this version focuses exclusively on contemplative practice while including recitation, which is essential for cultivation and realization. Alternatively, if one is pressed by official duties and unable to follow the full sequence of contemplative practice, it is also permissible to select and apply portions of it according to one's needs.]
The *Cundāmahāvidyārājñī-sūtra* states: "If there are lay or ordained bodhisattvas who have resolved upon bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva,
seeking swift liberation from birth and death, they must first enter the maṇḍala of the samaya-consecration,

receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts with firm resolve and without regression, take delight in the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts and practices, and cultivate them throughout the four modes of deportment."
Cultivate the four immeasurables and give rise to the four great vows. Only when all activities are performed with an undistracted mind may one enter this secret dharma-gate.
Upon first entering the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), one must further perform prostrations and repentance, take the precepts through self-vow, and rejoice while making aspirations.
Thereafter, one should engage in recitation (the subsequent stages of contemplative practice are established according to this sequence).

The Ritual of the Mandala (For the practitioner of mantra: before an image of the Buddha, observe the precepts and prepare offerings, burning incense and pure water. Therefore, one must accord with one’s own Vairocana-dharmadhātu and cultivate the ocean of the primordially existing Samantabhadra practices, so that inexhaustible function may swiftly manifest before one.

The ocean of the conduct of the wise is vast and boundless. Now, turning to contemplative practice, I shall briefly indicate five gates: first, the contemplation of all phenomena as being like dreams and illusions;

second, the contemplation of true suchness as transcending all marks; third, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; fourth, the contemplation of the infinite net of Indra.

The fifth is the contemplation of the unobstructed dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). First, regarding the contemplation that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions (which is precisely the contemplation of the dharma-realm as it is):

this means constantly contemplating that all phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are in their entirety unreal and are all like dreams and illusions. This observing wisdom (*prajñā*) itself is also like a dream and an illusion.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "For example, it is like seeing various different appearances within a dream. The world...

It is also thus; it is no different from a dream. Furthermore, it is said: "To deliver all sentient beings and cause them to know the Dharma—sentient beings are like illusions, and there is no difference between them and the understanding of illusion. Illusions have no sentient beings. Moreover, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way. Master Zhao said: "How empty!"
Delusory indeed are the three realms, for they lack substantiality; dreamlike and illusory are the six destinies, for they possess no reality.

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have clung to all phenomena as being truly existent, thereby giving rise to delusion and creating karma, causing them to circulate through the six destinies.

If one constantly contemplates that all fame, profit, enemies, and kin throughout the three realms and six paths of existence are entirely unreal, being like dreams and illusions, then love and hatred will naturally grow thin, and compassion and wisdom will naturally increase in clarity.
(This contemplation of dreams and illusions is called the "Contemplation of Arising Illusions to Eliminate Defilements" in the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* [Yuánjué shū];

in the Tiantai school, it is called the "Contemplation of the Provisional" [jiàguān], and is also termed "Cessation that Adapts to Conditions through Expedients. To clearly reflect and illuminate is called "contemplation" [guān]; to be tranquil and undisturbed is called "cessation" [zhǐ]. Thus, cessation is present within contemplation, and contemplation is fully contained within cessation; this is the dual cultivation of cessation and contemplation.)

This is due to destiny (*bhāgya*). The remaining methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* should be understood according to this principle. If a person, though they have faith and understanding in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), possesses heavy and thick afflictions (*kleśa*) such that they are unable to practice this "dream-and-illusion contemplation," they should instead practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

This refers to contemplating the five kinds of impurity of the body: first, impurity of the seed; second, impurity of the dwelling place; third, impurity of the self-substance; fourth, impurity of its own characteristics; and fifth, ultimate impurity. Tiantai said: "From the feet to the head, and from the head to the feet, one contemplates the body in succession, seeing that it is nothing but..."

One sees [the body] bloated, decaying, and putrefying; from the passages of excrement and urine, worms and pus flow out, its stench being more foul than that of a dead dog. Having finished observing one's own body, one then observes others, and finally observes the bodies of all sentient beings in the world, seeing that they are all impure. Alternatively, one performs the contemplation of the skeleton (*asthi-śaṅkalikā*).

One should first visualize the skin and flesh on the forehead of one’s own body rotting and falling away, seeing only white bones gradually extending from the narrow to the broad. One imagines the skin and flesh of the scalp rotting and falling away, seeing the white bone, and so on until the entire body is likewise visualized.

One sees white bones. Having seen one's own body, one further contemplates other people, gradually extending the contemplation to a single city, a single country, and eventually to the entire earth filled with skeletons. Then, reversing the process from broad to narrow, one focuses on a single body until only a small amount of white bone at the space between the eyebrows is seen.

By concentrating the mind on this single object and practicing in this manner, one eventually attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When this contemplation is perfected, all craving and attachment naturally vanish. Alternatively, one may practice the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which should be cultivated progressively from shallow to deep. First...

One must harmonize one's own breath so that it is neither constricted nor slippery, and with single-minded concentration, count the inhalations and exhalations. First count the inhalations, then the exhalations, from one to ten, beginning again at the end. Contemplate the mind as being fixed upon the counting, not allowing it to become distracted.

If you perceive your own mind, do so without applying effort; let it proceed spontaneously from one to ten while abiding in the counting of the breath. Furthermore, with single-mindedness, follow the breath as it enters and exits. When the breath enters, the mind follows it from the nose to the throat, then to the heart, and finally to the navel.

The thighs, the spleen, the shins, and even down to the toes. When the breath goes out, the mind also follows it. As the breath goes out and leaves the body, it extends for the distance of one span or one fathom; with single-minded focus, one constantly follows the inhalation and exhalation of the breath. If one becomes aware of the mind and the breath, they will naturally and spontaneously depend upon one another.

Nevertheless, one should further fix the attention solely between the eyebrows or at the tip of the nose, settling the mind there to observe the breath abiding in the body like a thread through a pearl. One should discern whether it is cold or warm, and whether it causes harm or benefit. If the body is perceived as serene and joyful, one should further carefully observe the subtle breath and contemplate the thirty-six impurities within and without the entire body.

Furthermore, one observes that the mental consciousness does not abide for even a single moment. By practicing in this way, one becomes aware of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath pervading all the pores; the eye of the mind opens and clarifies, and one clearly perceives the thirty-six internal substances and the various openings for parasites within the body.

Only then should one proceed to practice other meditative methods. There are further explanations, but fearing prolixity, I shall stop here. As stated in the sutras, contemplating the inhalation and exhalation is the gateway through which the Buddhas of the three periods enter the Path.

This is the first gate. Alternatively, one may practice the contemplation of the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). One must apply the mind to investigate: this present body is fundamentally without a self; it is merely a composite phenomenon of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Matter consists of the four elements: earth, water, fire, and wind.

Specifically, hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities are all the element of earth. Mucus, saliva, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of feces and urine are all the element of water. Warmth is the element of fire. Movement is the element of wind.

This wind turns. The mind consists of four categories: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. That which experiences is feeling; that which grasps images is perception; that which constructs is mental formation; and that which discerns is consciousness. Among these eight categories, which one is the self? If all of them were the self, [what would happen?]

Thus, there would be eight selves. Furthermore, within the physical form, there are three hundred and sixty segments of bone, each distinct from the others; the skin, hair, muscles, and sinews are different, as are the liver, heart, spleen, and kidneys. These various mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise each distinct: seeing is not hearing, and joy is not anger.

Since there are so many such entities, one does not know which one among them is definitively taken to be the self. If all of them were the self, then within these one hundred and eleven bodies, much confusion and disorder would arise.

Apart from these, there is no other separate phenomenon. When one turns this over and examines it to find the self, it cannot be found at all. One thus knows that this body is merely a provisional composite of various conditions, fundamentally devoid of a self. It is most excellent for a practitioner to constantly cultivate this contemplation day and night for the sake of all sentient beings.

Since beginningless time, one has clung to the body as the self. Because of cherishing this self, one greedily seeks fame and profit, desiring to bring honor and benefit to it; one feels anger toward objects that conflict with it, fearing they will harm or diminish it; and through the state of ignorance, one engages in irrational calculations.

Now, having constantly contemplated that this body is fundamentally without self, the three poisons naturally extinguish themselves. Once the three poisons are extinguished, one naturally leaves the three realms behind. Alternatively, when practicing the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), one must carefully observe that this body consists of the two factors of form and mind. Form comprises earth, water, fire, and wind; mind comprises sensation...

Regarding the eight factors—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—one should contemplate each one with true discernment: they all arise from conditions and possess no inherent nature; these eight factors are, in their very essence, emptiness. Beginners should practice such gates of contemplation according to their inclination, whether one, two, or even up to five types, and may cultivate them all.
Second is the contemplation of True Suchness as being beyond all marks (which is the contemplation of the Dharma-realm in accordance with principle); therein, one should settle the mind.

Furthermore, there are three gates. First, one constantly contemplates that throughout the entire dharma-realm there is only the single flavor of pure *tathatā* (suchness), which fundamentally lacks any differentiated phenomena. This contemplating wisdom is also the single flavor of *tathatā*.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unceasing. If one can understand them thus, the Buddhas are ever present before one. Furthermore...
The Seventh Patriarch Chan Master said: "That which is non-thoughtful thought is precisely the thought of True Suchness. The Sixth Patriarch explained non-thought (*amanasikāra*) as follows:
"Non" means the absence of all marks; "thought" means the thought of True Suchness. This is the contemplation of all phenomena, which is entirely True Suchness.
Although this contemplation is fundamentally devoid of the mark of contemplation, the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "Though one contemplates, there is nothing that can contemplate."

One should reflect that the *tathatā* (suchness) conceived herein is precisely the "non-relative true mind" (*atyantānapekṣa-tattva-citta*) taught in the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). This refers to the non-relative single mind (*ekacitta*), which completely pervades and is pure, allowing no room for any other deluded appearances;

these have been non-existent from the beginning. The non-relative true mind is fundamentally pure. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and quiescent; it is without grasping and without seeing. This emptiness is itself the Buddha; it cannot be apprehended through thought. The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:

"All phenomena, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names, and free from the characteristics of mental objects. They are ultimately equal, without change, and indestructible. Being solely this single mind, they are called *tathatā*. This refers to the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna (*mahāyāna-antaśāsana*).

In accordance with the delusions of sentient beings, it is taught that there is a physical body, as well as mountains, rivers, space, the great earth, and all phenomena of the world, so as to cause these beings to turn away from falsehood and return to the truth, thereby realizing that the physical body, mountains, rivers, space, the great earth, and all worldly phenomena are entirely of one flavor—the wondrously luminous true mind.

Now, within the Sudden Teaching, there is fundamentally no physical body, mountains, rivers, space, the great earth, or any worldly phenomena; they are fundamentally of one flavor, the absolute, peerless true mind. Thus, Qingliang said: "In total, he does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa), but only distinguishes the true nature.

This means one knows that what pervades the dharma-realm is fundamentally of one flavor, the absolute, peerless true mind—tranquil and pure, neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing. Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have failed to understand this mind and have been deluded.

Seeing various marks is like a person with an eye disease who mistakenly perceives flowers in the sky. The *Tujue jing* (Sūtra on Awakening through Contemplation) says: "To falsely identify the four great elements as the mark of one's own body, and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the mark of one's own mind, is like that diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky.

It further states: "If a Tathāgata, while practicing the stage of the causal ground, were to cultivate the path of a Pratyekabuddha, he would know these to be flowers in the sky; thus there would be no cyclic flow, nor would there be a body or mind undergoing birth and death. They do not exist because they are not created; they do not exist because their fundamental nature is non-existent.

A practitioner of this gate should constantly contemplate all phenomena as being of a single flavor—pure True Suchness (*tathatā*), fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. This is called the Samādhi of True Suchness, also called the Samādhi of One Practice, and also called the Samādhi of Non-arising. Second, if thoughts arise:

At that time, one simply gives rise to the mind of awakening. Therefore, the Seventh Patriarch said: "When a thought arises, awaken immediately; upon awakening, it is gone. This is the wondrous gate of cultivation; it lies solely in this.

This very mind of awakening is what is called *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). Although one gives rise to the mind of awakening here as well, fundamentally there is no characteristic of giving rise to awakening.

(For a practitioner of this gate, whenever mental thoughts arise at any time, simply giving rise to the mind of awakening is the essential and wondrous gate of cultivation. Third, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).

The mind is immediately at variance; the moment a thought stirs, one deviates from the truth. Simply let the mind rest without any point of attachment, and the principle will naturally be realized in its profound mystery.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and still; there is neither grasping nor seeing. This very emptiness is the Buddha; it cannot be conceived through discursive thought.
Furthermore, an ancient master said: "The true mark transcends speech and thought; True Suchness is beyond seeing and hearing. This is the place where the mind is settled."
The heterodox disciples say, and so forth: "This merely allows one's own original nature to illuminate itself;

no further newly arisen wisdom or understanding is produced. Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts.
Regarding these deluded minds, they do not seek to extinguish them. Abiding within the realm of delusive thought, they do not apply analytical knowledge. Regarding that which is non-existent..."

To understand [this] yet fail to discern the reality is not true understanding. Furthermore, the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha) said: "If one gives rise to a mind that performs mundane or holy deeds, these are not true practices.
To perform no deeds at all, such that the mind of practice has no point of attachment—this is called the Great Practice.

This gate takes the self-illumination of the original nature as its contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). For a practitioner of this gate, at all times the mind has no point of attachment; this is called true cultivation. Although one fully cultivates the myriad practices, within those myriad practices the mind has no point of attachment. Furthermore, regarding Chan...

The essential teachings transmitted by the Seven Patriarchs of the East and the West consist of three gates that encompass everything without exception. First is the Gate of Seeing Nature (*jìngxìng mén*). One must first realize the absolute, non-referential true mind. All delusive appearances are fundamentally non-existent; the true mind is primordially pure and is itself the Buddha, not something to be sought externally.

This refers precisely to the "one mind" of the aforementioned Sudden Teaching. Second is the Gate of Settling the Mind (*ānxīn mén*). This refers to the three methods previously mentioned, such as contemplating True Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth. Third is the Gate of Cultivating Practice (*fāxíng mén*). One must fully cultivate the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices.

To rely completely upon these three gates is what constitutes Right Meditation (*zhèng chán*). If even one gate is lacking, it becomes a biased view. Bodhidharma said: "My Dharma transmits the mind by means of the mind; it does not establish written words. This mind is the pure, fundamental nature of all sentient beings.

Awakening is also called Buddha-nature. Those who seek the Buddha-way must awaken to this mind; this is the Gate of Seeing Nature (*jìng-xìng mén*). It is further said: "To settle the mind in this way is what is meant by 'wall-contemplation' (*bì-guàn*). This causes the practitioner to abide in the True Principle, tranquil and non-active, resembling a wall that gives rise to no discrimination;

this is the Gate of Settling the Mind (*ān-xīn mén*). It is further said: "To initiate practice in this way is what is meant by the 'Four Practices': first, the Practice of Repaying Enmity. This means that when a practitioner undergoes suffering, they should reflect: 'From the distant past, I have [committed... "

Throughout many eons, they have abandoned the fundamental for the peripheral, wandering through various realms of existence. They have frequently given rise to resentment and hatred, committing infinite acts of harm and injury. Although there is no offense committed now, these are my karmic grudges from the past;

as the fruits of evil karma ripen, neither gods nor humans can prevent them, so I accept them with a willing heart and endure them without any complaint or grievance. As the Sūtra says: "When encountering suffering, one does not grieve. Why? Because of thorough understanding. Second, acting in accordance with conditions: this means that if a practitioner of the Way obtains superior rewards such as honor and fame, they should reflect to themselves: "All phenomena are..."

It arises from conditions. This is what was brought about by the causes I cultivated in the past; I have only now obtained it. When conditions are exhausted, it returns to nothingness. What cause for joy is there? Gain and loss follow conditions; the mind neither increases nor decreases. Unmoved by the wind of joy, the wind of anger does not arise. These are the three practices of non-seeking.

Worldly people are long lost in delusion, greedily attached everywhere—this is called "seeking. The wise realize the True Principle: they regard the world of desire and the two higher realms, with their nine abodes, as being like a burning house. Having a body is entirely suffering; who can find peace within them? Within these three realms...

"Without seeking, there is joy. A sutra states: "All seeking is suffering; non-seeking is joy. Fourth is the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*). This refers to the intrinsically pure true reality, which is designated as "Dharma. Since this rational nature is fundamentally free from all evils such as stinginess, one should accord with this rational nature by cultivating all manner of virtues, such as giving.

These four practices constitute the gate of initiating practice (*pravṛtti-mukha*). Furthermore, Master Caotang’s *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué shū*) also sets forth three gates that are largely identical to these:

first, awakening to the nature of perfect enlightenment, which is the single-flavor, pure true mind; second, generating the bodhicitta, which consists of great compassion, great wisdom, and great vows; and third, subsequently cultivating the bodhisattva practices, which refers to the dharmas of the six perfections and myriad practices. For those who study Chan, these three gates are of the utmost importance.

This is essential. If one does not practice the three gates in a complete manner, there is no way to depart from various false views. This is because the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the various schools of the Chan tradition from antiquity mostly corresponded only to the capacities and needs of their respective times; some spoke only of "seeing nature" (*jianxing*), some only of "settling the mind" (*anshin*), and some only of "arousing practice" (*fahang*).

Furthermore, within these practices of settling the mind and arousing practice, there were again many different paths, such as clarifying only a single path, and so forth. Now, if the mind thoroughly penetrates these various gates, only then will one, upon reading the various Chan teachings, understand the ultimate aim and conclusion of each. 3.

The Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Phenomena and Principle (i.e., the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction between Phenomena and Principle): This refers to constantly contemplating all defiled phenomena...
All phenomena of purity and defilement arise dependently and lack intrinsic nature; they are entirely the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is entirely all phenomena of purity and defilement.
It is like observing that waves are entirely moisture, and moisture is entirely waves. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Although one contemplates all dharmas..."

While their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-arising, one further contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed (the principle does not obstruct phenomena;

just as the nature of moisture is one, it does not obstruct the manifestation of many waves). Although one contemplates these causes and conditions and the retributions of good and evil karma, [they remain non-arising].

And yet, even while recollecting, the nature [of mind] cannot be apprehended (the fact does not obstruct the principle; it is like how, though waves are many, they do not obstruct the fact that they are entirely of the nature of moisture). If one practices the three contemplations within the provisional emptiness:

To contemplate that all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature, being entirely empty in their very essence—this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is like observing an image in a mirror, which has no substantial reality whatsoever.

To contemplate that although all phenomena exist, they are unreal and are all like dreams or illusions—this is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*). It is like observing an image in a mirror, which appears to exist but lacks reality. To contemplate that all phenomena are entirely of one taste, the wondrously luminous true mind—this refers to the vast true mind as explained in the aforementioned Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).

This is the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*). It is like observing a clear mirror. Regarding these three contemplations, one may practice them by focusing on a single gate, or practice them gradually and sequentially, or practice them all simultaneously; this depends on the capacity of the practitioner. Fourth is the contemplation of the inexhaustible Indra’s net.

This refers to the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm of Non-obstruction in All Affairs (*shishi wuai fajie guan*). Within this, five gates are briefly presented: first, the Gate of Prostration; second, the Gate of Offering.
1. The Gate of Repentance; 2. The Gate of Making Vows; 3. The Gate of Recitation. Regarding the first, the Gate of Prostration:
this means that one visualizes throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm—within every atom and every buddha-field—the inexhaustible triple gem of the Indra-net.

Before each of these, there is an equally inexhaustible body of oneself, also like an Indra-net. Each individual body prostrates before each of the inexhaustible triple gems of the Indra-net. Before each and every triple gem...
Before each of these jewels, one performs the infinite-body prostrations of the self-manifesting Indra’s net. Furthermore, contemplate this single gate:

it shall continue until the end of the future, never ceasing, with mindfulness and mindfulness succeeding one another without interruption, and with the actions of body, speech, and mind free from weariness or fatigue.

(As Qingliang said: "If one does not enter this contemplation, one will merely exhaust oneself in vain. Alternatively, one may first enter the 'Gate of Purity,' imagining that the entire Dharma-realm is entirely Vairocana Buddha, or [the Buddhas such as] Cundī; before each individual Honored One, one should first imagine performing prostrations with a single body.")

If it is still difficult to enter, first visualize ten honored Buddhas. Before each honored one, perform one prostration. Once you have become somewhat proficient in this practice, gradually increase the number to a hundred, a thousand, and even to infinity (the subsequent practices follow this method).

Regarding making offerings, repentance, making vows, and recitation, all are detailed within the section on contemplative practice. As for the "Inexhaustible Contemplation of the Indra’s Net" (*Indrajāla-anantya-vipaśyanā*): this refers to the pearls strung upon an Indra’s net, where their radiating lights reflect one another.

The light of a single pearl enters a thousand pearls, and the light of those thousand pearls enters back into the single pearl; furthermore, the light of that single pearl mutually contains and encompasses them all, layer upon layer without end. When performing this contemplation, the various forms of worship and reverence practiced in each section [are integrated].

All of these pervade the Dharma-realm. One may perform this visualization while seated; or when prostrating to the Buddha, burning incense, offering flowers, repenting, or making vows, one may briefly enter this contemplation; or when reciting scriptures, it is most excellent to first complete this visualization before reciting.

Even if one lacks incense, flowers, and the like, simply joining the palms and entering this gateway of contemplation yields merit that is likewise inexhaustible. Since the aforementioned five gateways are thus, the remaining practices should be cultivated accordingly.
Regarding the cultivation of the contemplation of "identity" (*xi xiang ji guan*), there are four propositions: the first is "one is identical to one."
That is to say: first, when one contemplates that a single hair is identical to a single ear, at that same time, the single ear is likewise identical to the single hair.
Second, all things are identical to one; third, one is identical to all—these two phrases should be contemplated as a unified whole. That is to say:

fourth, when one contemplates that all sensory objects (*dharmas*) are identical to a single Buddha, at that same time, the single Buddha is likewise identical to all sensory objects. Fourth, all things are identical to one.

"Universal" (qie) means that when one contemplates all persons as being simultaneously all Buddhas, and all Buddhas as being simultaneously all persons—within each of these phrases, one should apply this same method of contemplation by analogy to all dharmas. If one practices the contemplation of mutual inclusion, there are likewise four phrases.
The first is "one encompassing one, one including one": this means contemplating that one person encompasses one Buddha and includes one [Buddha].

It is as follows: First, one enters into a single Bodhisattva; just as a mirror in the east reflects and carries the image from a mirror in the south into a mirror in the west, so too does one carry all things into a single [Bodhisattva].
This refers to contemplating how a single flower reflects and carries all rivers into it, and then entering into a single mountain. Second, one carries a single thing into all;
this refers to contemplating how all things reflect and carry a single thing into all of them. Third, one carries all things into all; this refers to contemplating all...
One takes a single atom and, encompassing it, brings it into all pores of the skin. Fourth, one encompasses everything and, encompassing it, brings it into everything;
that is, one contemplates taking all trees, encompassing all spirits within them, and bringing them into all oceans.
Within each phrase, all dharmas should be contemplated according to this analogy. This characteristic is "mutual inclusion. This is the second contemplation.
In each successive contemplation, there are further general and specific observations; as these involve many repeated cycles of observing the mind, I fear they would be too prolix to show here.
Simply cultivate and refine with single-minded devotion, and you will naturally attain clear understanding. Thus, the Preface to the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* by Lord Pei states:

"Provided that the student merges this realm with their own mind, the wisdom of the mind will immediately become luminous, and one will personally perceive its inexhaustible meaning; it does not depend on exhaustive [exegesis]."
Regarding the general teachings (*pāṭha*), the sections and divisions are set out in detail.

If one practices the "contemplation of simultaneous and complete correspondence," then by contemplating a single phenomenon (*dharma*), one simultaneously and completely fulfills all phenomena within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Other profound gateways should be understood according to this principle.

If there are those who delight in practicing the three contemplations and three cessations of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), it is said that when a practitioner contemplates a single person, they immediately accomplish the three.

Contemplating the three types of cessation: let us consider a single human body to fully clarify the three truths. The provisional appearance of the human body exists; therefore, it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The human body arises through conditions and is non-existent; the nature of its form is essentially empty; therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The provisional appearance of the human body has no separate self-nature; its entire substance is the truth of tranquil illumination; this is called the middle-way truth (*madhyamā-satya*). Now, as for the essence of these three truths...

Employing non-obstruction, one contemplates emptiness and existence as mutually interpenetrating: they are three while being one, and one while being three. Such is the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Relying upon these three truths, the practitioner’s contemplation constitutes the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) and the three cessations (*trividha-śamatha*).

That is to say, when the practitioner’s mind contemplates the human body as a provisional form existing like an illusion, it is called the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*). When this contemplating mind realizes the provisional nature of forms and thereby abandons the attachment to substantial existence, it is called [the contemplation of the empty].

One then allows the mind to rest according to conditions. Furthermore, contemplating that the physical form and substance of the human body are entirely empty is called the "contemplation of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

When this contemplative mind realizes the emptiness of form, one becomes free from the attachment to the substantial reality of the physical body; this is called "stopping by means of the true nature of substance" (*tattva-śamatha*).

Furthermore, contemplating that every part of the human body is entirely the Middle Way’s true nature is called the "contemplation of the Middle Way" (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*). This contemplative mind is thus free from the attachment to the existence of characteristics.

And by abandoning the attachment to emptiness as a substantial entity, one is said to be "distant from the discrimination of the two extremes. Observing the mind in this manner, within a single thought-moment, the three truths manifest simultaneously;
