Therefore, in my *Cizhao Jichan* (The Compassionate Illumination Collection of Repentance), fearing that people might become attached to their nature and lose sight of the principle, I stated: "I vow to deliver the sentient beings of self-nature; I vow to sever the afflictions of self-nature..."
I vow to sever affliction; I vow to study the Dharma-gate of self-nature; I vow to accomplish the Buddha-way of self-nature.

These four lines directly clarify the true principle, desiring that all people, within their own nature, bring to an end all deluded thoughts and sentient beings—namely, the various false and confused conceptions, as well as minds of greed, ignorance, jealousy, anger, and malice—and thus cause them [to attain liberation].

To give rise to the great vow is to deliver oneself by means of one's own nature. Furthermore, within this self-nature, one must sever all afflictions—namely, the defilements of worldly toil, karmic consciousness, perverse thoughts, and evil intentions—which are like floating clouds that obscure and cover self-nature so that its radiance does not manifest.
Therefore, one causes the great vow to arise in order to sever these for oneself, ensuring they never arise again. Moreover, within self-nature...

Within this, one studies all dharma-gates—namely, the immeasurable dharma-gates of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), compassion, wisdom, practice, and vows—and thus causes the great vow to arise.
One awakens oneself and cultivates oneself, never falling back, until reaching Bodhi. One does not consider a small attainment sufficient.
Furthermore, within one's own nature, one has confidence that there is a Buddha; one gives rise to the great vow and constantly [cultivates] for oneself.

Contemplating and observing, one vows to attain the Bodhi of Buddhahood oneself. This is the compassionate and earnest heart of the "old woman" (the Buddha), clearly opening a gateway for future generations.
It requires only that you all have self-confidence and self-acceptance;
by entering through this very point, you will awaken to your own nature, realize that Amitābha is but the pure land of the mind, enter the realm of all Buddhas, and achieve the unsurpassed.
Bodhi! Alas, the virtuous people of this world do not understand this meaning; they seek it elsewhere outside themselves.
How is this different from carrying a divine pearl while wandering about begging?
Cizhao said: "If there is practice without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary. If there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty.
Without practice and without aspiration, one dwells in vain within Jambudvīpa. With both practice and aspiration, one enters directly into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is the very foundation for Buddhas and patriarchs to cultivate the karma of purity. Observing the present age, those who have faith and take refuge in the Buddhist assembly do so either because of illness and suffering,"
Thus they resolve their minds. Some do so to repay their parents; some to protect and maintain their homes; some to observe the fasts out of fear of transgressions.

Though they possess faith, they lack practice and vows. Though they claim to recite the Buddha’s name, they do not reach its fundamental root. All such cultivation of virtuous conditions is merely for the sake of returning [to this world]; such sincere aspirations are rare.
It is only when one resolves their mind to recite the Buddha’s name for the sake of their own birth and death that they truly seek [liberation].

Those who take birth in the Pure Land often offer incense and candles at the altar with prayers and dedications that merely express offerings to the divine spirits for the purpose of eliminating calamities and prolonging life.
Consequently, this contradicts the original intent of the sutra recitations and repentance rites, and does not accord with the fundamental vows of the Buddhas.
Even if one spends an entire lifetime in cultivation and recitation, failing to understand the underlying principles and applying effort in error, this is called "spending the whole day [in vain]."
One may count another’s treasures, yet not receive even half a coin for oneself.
Now, those who hold the *Cundī* mantra and make vows—whether for the sake of accomplishing worldly conditions—it will not hinder them, provided they ultimately return to the right vow.
This is what is meant by "perfectly cultivating pure karma."

The unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, which arises from the aspiration for enlightenment, is called *bodhi*. If one generates this mind, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. The *Pure Conduct Dharma Gate* states:
"In practicing the Pure Land, one must properly generate the aspiration. If it is for one's own sake, one loathes the five turbidities and yearns for the nine grades [of rebirth]; then..."

To contravene the bodhicitta is the practice of a śrāvaka; it should not be generated. However, if one generates the mind of great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, seeking rebirth in that land with the hope of swift accomplishment, and traverses the ten directions through the power of the Path and supernormal faculties to rescue and deliver all beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood—this accords with the bodhicitta.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva; it should indeed be generated. Now, I exhort [you] toward purity.
The Flow of High Karma. Those who wish to benefit themselves and others must first resolve their minds and establish their vows.
Before the Triple Gem, they should reverently offer incense and flowers and, with a sincere heart, make this vow: "Namo Buddha, Namo Dharma, Namo Sangha.

From this day forth, I, [Name], disciple, give rise to this Great Mind. I shall not seek for myself the blessings and rewards of the realms of humans or devas, nor those of the Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas..."
Hearing this, even bodhisattvas at all stages of the provisional vehicles resolve their minds toward Bodhi solely by relying on the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle.

They vow that they, along with their parents of this life, their parents of many lifetimes, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm—whether enemies or kin—may be reborn together in the Pure Land and all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Thus, three times...

It is said that this mind must be awakened from time to time, yet it should be so every single day. This is why Sudhana realized the fruit in a single lifetime, and the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood at the age of eight.
By awakening the mind while in hell, one suddenly transcends the ten stages; by forming the resolve as a novice monk, one already surpasses the Two Vehicles.
It may be said that with a single breath one returns to the source; how profound is the grace that moistens all things!
Regarding the three types of pure karma, the third—generating the bodhicitta—is designated in the commentary as the uncommon karma of the Mahāyāna.
This means it differs from the resolve generated by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). For "bodhi" refers to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
it is the ultimate fruit and virtue of all Buddhas and the buddha-nature that is the fundamental source of sentient beings. To cultivate the Mahāyāna...
This refers to the arousal of the self-nature based on the four truths of the perfect and sudden unconditioned (wu-zuo) teaching; these are the Four Great Vows.

Specifically, it means arousing the bodhicitta, which is the foremost of all practices and the beginning of treading the Path. It encompasses the entirety from start to finish and must never be abandoned for even a moment.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The bodhicitta is like a seed, for it is able to produce all the dharmas of the Buddhas. Thus, the bodhicitta...
It is like a fertile field, for it can cause the pure dharmas of sentient beings to grow.
The bodhicitta is like the great earth, for it can support all worlds. The bodhicitta is like pure water, for it can wash away the stains of all afflictions.
The bodhicitta is like a great wind, for it pervades the world without obstruction.
Therefore, the bodhicitta is like a blazing fire, for it can burn away the fuel of all worldly views. Question:

Since the principle of bodhi is inherently perfect and complete by its very nature, why is it necessary to give rise to the resolve [for awakening], which involves the production of conceptual thoughts? Answer: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva knows that the nature of the mind is itself bodhi, yet is still able to generate the great bodhicitta, this is called bodhi..."
"Sa. Furthermore, the leading Bodhisattva said: "Within that which is sought for nothing, I nevertheless seek it. Knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, I give rise to the bodhicitta.
The True Suchness (tathatā) realized is such that there is no wisdom outside of it; yet it can give rise to wondrous wisdom. Wisdom is such that there is no Suchness outside of it.
It simultaneously illuminates and simultaneously negates; neither preserved nor extinguished. It is non-dual, yet dual—wisdom and principle."
The self is both two and non-dual; subject and object are both quiescent.
One practices the six perfections and the myriad deeds in unison.
As for the "six perfections," they are: giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—these are the six *pāramitās*.
If a person who recollects the Buddha focuses exclusively on the cultivation of samādhi and seeks to transcend the world, they must attain ultimate goodness.
One must know that the six pāramitās and myriad practices do not go beyond the single mind; within this single mind, all dharmas are fully present.

It is like having bathed in the great ocean and thus having used the waters of all rivers; it is like making a pill from ten thousand kinds of incense—if one burns a single pill, the full flavor of all the ingredients is present.
It is like a person who takes up treasures and obtains the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*);
from this, all manner of jewels arise inexhaustibly. How do we know this is so? By upholding even a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha," one attains *samādhi*.

Within a single thought-moment, one accords with the Principle (*tattva*), and all phenomena manifest before one; the six perfections and the myriad practices are all fully complete. As for giving, the mind is free from...
Through non-attachment, one upholds the precepts; through patience, both subject and object are forgotten; through diligence, the mind is uninterrupted;
through meditative concentration, both movement and stillness are quiescent; and through wisdom, not even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization is established.

Thus, within a single act of deliverance, there arise immeasurable acts of deliverance; within each act of deliverance, they are like the lattice of Indra’s net. One need only know that this is the fundamental nature of the one mind.

Emptiness is spontaneous; therein all practices are fully perfected. Therefore, the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, the eighty-four thousand wisdoms, and the eighty-four thousand merits are all born from a single thought—the mind that recollects the Buddha.
As the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla says in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "O Son of the Buddha, at all times, by skillfully employing the mind, one attains the One [Vehicle]."
All supreme and wondrous merits may be described as the single nature perfectly penetrating all natures, and the single dharma universally harmonizing with all dharmas.
According to the *Nianfo Samādhi Mantra* and its meditative practices (*samādhi*), although the methods of recitation differ, they constitute the perfect cultivation of the myriad practices.
First: Resolving to Be Born in the Pure Land.
Question: Regarding those among the people of today who practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name), many are born in the Western Paradise, yet few attain Buddhahood. Why is this? Answer:
This is because there are three [conditions]. First, although one may recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth, if the mind is not virtuous, one will not attain rebirth there.

I exhort all people of the world: since you are reciting the Buddha’s name, you must follow what the Buddha has taught. You must accumulate merit and cultivate blessings; you must be filial toward your parents;
you must serve your sovereign with loyalty; you must love one another as brothers; you must respect one another as husband and wife; you must reach [the goal]...
Be sincere, truthful, and honest. You must be gentle and patient; you must be impartial and upright; you must practice secret kindness and skillful means;
you must have compassion for all beings. Do not kill living creatures; do not insult those beneath you; do not oppress the common people.
Whenever an unwholesome thought arises, exert yourself in the recitation of the Buddha’s name with the firm resolve to drive that unwholesome thought away. Only in this way is it truly so.

Those who practice nianfo will certainly attain Buddhahood. However, if one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth while the mind is filled with random thoughts, one will not achieve rebirth in the Pure Land.
I exhort all people in the world: when practicing nianfo, you must restrain the restless monkey of the mind and the unruly horse of the will.
Every word must be distinct; every thought must be clearly attended. It is as if one were personally in the Western Land, facing Amitābha Buddha, not daring to let the mind wander.

Only in this way is one a true practitioner of *nien-fo*; such a person will certainly attain Buddhahood. Third, though one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth, the heart only wishes for wealth and status in a future life;
or one says, "We ordinary beings cannot possibly reach the Western Land," and so forth. There is no self [in such a state].
To merely seek to ensure that one does not lose their human form in future lives is contrary to the Buddha’s intent.
The Buddha points you toward rebirth in the Western Paradise, yet you yourself are unwilling to be reborn there; for this reason, you will not attain rebirth. I urge all people in the world:

those who recite the Buddha's name must resolve to seek birth in the Western Paradise and refrain from harboring doubts. Consider, for example, how even the wealth, nobility, and blessings of the celestial palaces come to an end.
...will surely fall. How much more so for human wealth and honor, which can last but a short time?

If you say that as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) you have no share in the Western Land, then it follows that all sages and worthies were once ordinary persons. How do you know that they did not take birth in the Western Land?
Thus, you should immediately give rise to a vast mind, establish a firm resolve, and vow to be reborn there, to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and attain [liberation].
The supreme fruit is the vast salvation of sentient beings; only such a person is truly one who practices the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo) and will certainly attain Buddhahood.
For a practitioner of true faith, it is essential to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded focus, recite one phrase of "Amitābha Buddha. This single thought-moment alone is my Original Teacher; this single thought-moment alone—
This is precisely the transformation Buddha. This single thought-moment is the valiant general who shatters hell;
this single thought-moment is the precious sword that slays the multitudes of evil; this single thought-moment is the bright lamp that illuminates darkness;
this single thought-moment is the great ship that ferries one across the sea of suffering; this single thought-moment is the efficacious remedy for escaping birth and death. Only...
This single thought-moment is the path for exiting the triple world. This very thought-moment is the original-nature Amitābha.
This very thought-moment reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only. One need only remember this phrase "Amitābha Buddha" within one's mindfulness; do not let it be lost.
Let it be ever-present in every thought-moment, never departing from the mind. Thus, there is nothing to be done. So it is.
One should be mindful of the presence of affairs; likewise, one should be mindful of peace and happiness; likewise, one should be mindful of the suffering of illness;

likewise, one should be mindful of birth; likewise, one should be mindful of death. Thus, with such single-minded mindfulness, clear and unclouded, what further need is there to ask others for the path home?
It may be said that the journey of the boat rests entirely upon the helmsman; those who attain this wisdom travel together toward Nirvana.

Bannu. In the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the King of Vows, made ten great vows at the final assembly in the Jeta Grove. He attained rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"O King, each and every one of these vows states: 'As far as the realm of space extends, and as far as the realm of sentient beings extends, may these great vows of mine never come to an end.

When such a person approaches the end of life, at the final moment when all their faculties are utterly disintegrated and all their power and majesty are completely lost—whether it be ministers, high officials, the interior or exterior of the palace, elephants, horses, or chariots..."
Mounting this vehicle, with its treasures and hidden storehouses, he shall no longer be followed by anything else; only this King of Vows shall never abandon him.
At all times, it shall lead him from the front, and within a single kṣaṇa, he shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss. Upon arrival, he shall immediately behold Amitābha Buddha.
That person shall see for themselves that they have been born within a lotus flower and receive a prophecy of enlightenment from the Buddha; having received this prophecy, they shall attain it.

Thus it has been for incalculable kalpas. Throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds in the ten directions, by the power of wisdom, he has benefited sentient beings according to their mental dispositions.

He has even been able to rescue sentient beings from the great ocean of afflictions and suffering, causing them to escape and all attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The *Zhenyuan shu* states: Question—

Why is it that one does not seek rebirth in the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) but instead aspires for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Jile*)? The answer is that there are four reasons. First, because there are those with whom [Amitābha] has a karmic affinity.

Second, because he desires to cause sentient beings to rely upon him with a single-minded devotion. Third, because [the Pure Land] is not separate from the Flower Treasury World. Fourth, because [Amitābha] is none other than the Original Teacher (Śākyamuni).
The *Xingyuan Chao* states: "Regarding 'having a karmic affinity,' Amitābha’s vows are profound; he specifically receives and guides the people of this Sahā world. Relying...

Regarding the first point on "Sentiment": If one hears that all ten directions are wondrous and that this and that are mutually interpenetrating, then the beginner's mind will become vast and茫然 (mángmáng—vast and bewildered), having nothing upon which to rely.
Therefore, as a skillful means, one guides them by saying they do not depart from the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

Although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is but ten trillion Buddha-lands away from here, the Buddha-fields within the Flower Treasury World are as numerous as motes of dust; thus, one does not depart from it. This refers to our Original Teacher.
Regarding this, the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Sūtra* states: "Or there are those who see the Buddha Amitāyus surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others.
The Commentary (*Śū*) judges this, saying: "This praises the virtues of the Honored One Vairocana. The Commentary further states: "The Flower Treasury World-Ocean is entirely the realm of Vairocana;
although the Buddha Amitāyus is ten trillion [worlds] away, he has not yet transcended the midst of the world-system (*kṣetra-vyañjana*)."

Is this not the Original Teacher (the Buddha) manifesting different transformations according to names? Master Daocun said: "The *Puxian Xingyuan Zan* (The Vow of Samantabhadra’s Practices and Vows) is a means for the circulation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Why, then, within the ocean of worlds, does it specifically point toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*)? Having already attained faith and understanding in the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanzong*),"

While rebirth in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions is possible, the conclusion that one must return specifically to the Western Land (Sukhāvatī) must surely have a profound underlying meaning. The answer is as follows:

After Samantabhadra had expounded the King of Vows for the ocean-like assembly of Sudhana, he concluded by directing them toward the West; this was because he intended it for those who possess the complete understanding of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).
They enter the wisdom of Mañjuśrī and cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra; their merit and wisdom, as well as phenomena and principle, all accord with the *dharmadhātu*.

Although these people of great resolve have attained a wondrous awakening to original luminosity and are suddenly equal to the various sages, their power and function are as yet not fully sufficient or complete.

Thus, until they achieve [Buddhahood], they temporarily rely upon the Pure Land to draw near to Amitābha and his ocean-like assembly, for the sake of universally benefiting sentient beings. Until they reach that point...
The Buddha said: "Therefore, the Sūtra states: 'I personally beheld the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light manifest before me, and he bestowed upon me the prediction of Bodhi.

Having received that prediction from the Tathāgata, I have manifested countless transformation bodies; with hundreds of koṭis of vast and great powers of wisdom pervading the ten directions, I universally benefit the realms of all sentient beings.
This is precisely the meaning of Cundī’s vow to dedicate her merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land."
According to the Cundi Pure Karma Contemplation Gate, it is identical and no different from the Avataṃsaka Dharma-realm Contemplation Gate;
both are the pure Dharmakāya of Vairocana. It is certain that by clarifying the direct cause, one will inevitably attain the direct fruit.
Yet there are those today who do not comprehend the principle of the Dharma-realm, yet insist on seeking the formless outside of forms.
This is not a matter of negating existence to achieve realization; rather, one would inevitably become mired in quiescence and sink into emptiness. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"To be detached from all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and to inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness—this is still merely a conceptual reflection of dharmas."

If one recites the mantra or upholds the name, these faults will not arise. This is because when contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is in accord with the path, one will necessarily enter the Dharma-realm of Vairocana;
this has already been fully set forth in the *Xianmi yuantong* (The Perfect Penetration of Exoteric and Esoteric).
Furthermore, as Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna proclaimed in his *Praise of Cundī*: "One who constantly recites the accumulation of Cundī’s merits with a tranquil mind..."
It is further said: "Encountering this wish-fulfilling jewel, one will certainly obtain that which is 'unequaled' (*asama-sama*).
Now, that which is 'unequaled' is the true fruit of Bodhi; and the tranquil mind is the true cause of Bodhi.

This means that while one constantly recites [the mantra] with a tranquil mind, it has never been heard that the practice of recitation hinders meditative stillness (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). However, there are also those who seek only worldly benefits and merit.
Those who do not seek the causes of wisdom are weighed down by worldly sentiments too heavily; they cannot avoid the reproach of returning the pearl after buying the casket.
Is it not the case that the *cintāmaṇi* jewel merely brings about the fulfillment of worldly blessings? Therefore, I have appended this section on pure karma.
I pray that all you virtuous ones will resolve to attain Bodhicitta, lest you conceal the pearl within your robes and fail to realize this excellent opportunity.
It is appropriate. Regarding the ritual for making offerings to the Buddha and benefiting sentient beings:

for one who prays for the Way, if they do not make supreme offerings to the Triple Gem and rescue the four classes of living beings below, there will be no cause for their merit and wisdom to increase.
Now, from within this Secret Treasury, I extract this essential and sublime gateway, hoping that the fourfold assembly will rely upon and practice it.
Those who wish to make offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha should first prostrate themselves fully before an image of the Triple Gem,
universally bowing to the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha throughout the entire Dharmadhātu, while reciting the Mantra of Universal Prostration seven times.
Pervasive. The mantra is: Oṃ Vajra-mudrā.
By the inconceivable power of this mantra, one naturally appears before the inexhaustible Triple Gem throughout the entire Dharmadhātu;

in each instance, one’s own body is present, and all perform prostrations and service. (This should be done whenever one reaches the morning or evening [services], or when entering a temple to worship the Buddha, etc.)

At that time, one should first recite this mantra. Then, using food, drink, incense, flowers, and whatever other items can be prepared according to one's means, as well as the vessels containing the food and drink, seal them all with the Universal Auspicious Seal (the right thumb and ring finger are pressed together while the remaining three fingers are extended).
Recite the Mantra for Purifying the Dharmadhātu twenty-one times to empower them. The mantra is as follows:
By reciting the syllable *kḷm*, through the power of mantra-consecration and mudrā, the food, drink, utensils, and so forth become naturally pure, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Next, recite the "Mantra for Transforming Food through Immeasurable Majestic Virtue, Sovereign Radiance, and Supreme Wondrous Power" twenty-one times. The mantra is as follows:
Namo sarvatathāgatavajrāgrī oṃ saṃbhara saṃbhara hūṃ.
By the power of this empowerment, the food and drink and so forth are immediately transformed into the various exquisite flavors of the celestial delicacies of the devas.

Offer this as an act of worship to fulfill the Three Jewels of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, offer praise and exhortation, and rejoice in all accumulated merit.
Finally, form the mudrā for manifesting offerings (join the palms at the heart; interlace the fingers with the right over the left, then place them upon the crown of the head).
Recite the mantra for the offering of emanation twenty-one times. The mantra is:
Oṃ. By reciting the syllable Oṃ, through the inconceivable power of the mantra and the mudrā, it naturally pervades the entire dharmadhātu.

There are inexhaustible offerings: incense, flowers, lamps, candles, banners, flags, parasols, canopies, robes, bedding, pavilions, palaces, music, song, dance, and various other implements for making offerings.
All these are offered throughout the entire Dharma-realm to the infinite Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as to the various devas.

(If one lacks food, drink, incense, or flowers, simply before a Buddha image, form this mudrā with the hands and recite this mantra; then naturally there will be inexhaustible offerings pervading everywhere.)
This is for making offerings to the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the Dharma-realm.
If one gives to the various sages, having filled a vessel to the brim with food and drink, one should recite the aforementioned mantra for transforming food twenty-eight times.
If cast into pure flowing water, it immediately transforms into exquisite food for celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*).

It is offered to hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of sages as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Those sages, having received this empowered food, each achieves the fundamental vows and all virtuous merits [they desire].
(If there are sons or daughters of good family who empower food with this secret mantra and bestow it upon those sages, they will be able to [attain] longevity in the present life...)

Life shall be prolonged; merit, virtue, and peace shall be secured. Whatever the mind perceives through sight and hearing shall be correctly understood and purified. One will fully accomplish these qualities, such that the majesty of Brahmā will render all enemies and adversaries incapable of causing harm.
If one intends to provide sustenance for hungry ghosts, at every dawn and at all times, there shall be no obstacles whatsoever.
Take a clean vessel and fill it with a small amount of pure water; place a little rice and various cakes or foods therein.

Holding the vessel with the left hand, form the Jewel Hand Mudrā (pressing the thumb against the index, middle, and little fingers, while extending the ring finger) to stir the food above and bestow the *ṛṣi-bhojana* (food of the sages); perform this mudrā as well. Then recite the aforementioned mantra for transforming food.
Recite this seven times. Having performed the empowerment, then invoke the names of the four Tathāgatas:

Namo to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna (who can eliminate the karma of stinginess and greed of hungry ghosts, so that they obtain the perfection of merit and virtue). Namo to the Tathāgata Suvarṇavarṇa-gātra (who can destroy the ugly forms of hungry ghosts, so that they obtain the fullness of physical marks).

Namo to the Tathāgata Vipulaśarīra (who can cause the throats and gullets of hungry ghosts to become wide and large, so that all food offered to them is entirely sufficient). Namo to the Tathāgata Vigatabhaya.
[This rite] can eliminate all fears of the hungry ghosts and enable one to leave the realm of ghosts. Having recited the names of the four Tathāgatas, snap your fingers seven times.
Take the food vessel and, on clean ground—or upon a clean stone, a raw-food stand, or in a clean vessel—pour it out with your arm extended. Having performed this offering:

Before hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of hungry ghosts, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the four directions, there shall be seven times seven *droṇas* of food from the kingdom of Magadha before each one.
Having received this food, they shall all be fully satiated; they shall entirely abandon the realm of hungry ghosts and be reborn in the heavens.

(If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who constantly empower food with this secret mantra and the names of the four Tathāgatas, and bestow it upon the hungry ghosts, they will be able to...)

They will be endowed with immeasurable merit. Those of short life shall have their lifespans extended; those of meager fortune shall see their merit and prosperity increase. Furthermore, they shall obtain a fresh and radiant complexion and possess powerful majesty. They will swiftly fulfill the *dānapāramitā*.

All non-humans, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and various malevolent spirits shall stand in awe of such a person and dare not harm them. If one wishes to offer water, take a handful of water and recite the Amṛta mantra over it seven times.
Scatter it into the air, and every single drop of that water shall immediately transform into ten *shu* of sweet nectar.
Dew. All hungry ghosts may drink from it without any deficiency, and all shall be fully satisfied.
The mantra for the nectar is: *Namo surūpāya tathāgatāya tadyathā oṃ suru suru pā*.
*rasuruvara rasuru svāhā*. (The *Maṇḍala-śāstra* states:

"Now, for one who practices the Way, the primary aim is to pray for and bring about [blessings]. If above one does not make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, where can one exercise wisdom in seeking bodhi?
If below one does not rescue the various spirits and hungry ghosts, where can one practice compassion to achieve sarvajña (omniscience)? Those with faith should not neglect this practice.")

If one wishes to benefit all sentient beings, whenever it rains, one should arouse the mind of great compassion, look upward toward the sky, and recite the Amṛta mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara twenty-one times.
All sentient beings touched by those raindrops will have all their evil karma and heavy transgressions completely extinguished, and they shall all obtain benefit and happiness. Furthermore,

If one recites this dhāraṇī, all transgressions committed in the past or present—such as the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, the slandering of the Vaipulya sūtras, and the sins of an icchantika—will be entirely extinguished without remainder.
One’s body and mind will become light and agile, and one’s wisdom will become clear and penetrating.
Whether by body or speech, they are able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings who have extensively committed all manner of crimes, such as the *ānantarya* offenses, should they encounter the person of this Vidyādhara and their body be briefly illuminated by his presence, or suddenly engage in conversation with him, [they will be liberated].
Or upon hearing the sound of these words, all the karmic obstacles of that person will be completely extinguished.
The mantra is as follows: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya | bhagavate mahāsattvāya* ||
Mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā oṃ dune dune kādune svāhā. (For those who prefer the abbreviated version, they should recite only from the syllable *oṃ* onwards.
The portion preceding *oṃ* is the verse of homage; *oṃ* and what follows constitute the core mantra.

If this dhāraṇī is inscribed upon all sound-producing objects such as bells, drums, and gongs—whether sounded by striking, blowing, or shaking—all sentient beings who hear these sounds will be completely purified. At the end of their lives, they shall be reborn in the Pure Land of the West. [In the mantra, *kāru*...]

*Nīkāya* and above constitute the Great Compassion Mantra (Dabei Zhou), comprising the first eight lines. (The omission of the character *he* [ha] in the opening line is merely due to differences in translation.

Regarding the various mantras for making offerings to the Buddhas and benefiting sentient beings mentioned above, if one is unable to recite or transcribe each of them individually, it is also permissible to use the Cundī Mantra for all purposes.
Thus, the *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi-sūtra* states: "This Cundī mantra is like a wish-fulfilling jewel; if one practices..."
People may employ this in various circumstances, and in all cases they shall achieve success.
This concludes the third fascicle of the *Cundī-vimala-karmānta*.
